title: 06. Memory, State & HITL: LangChain / LangGraph Checkpointers: Complete Explanations and Examples 3/4: What you must add before a production
summary: Implement explicit schema migrations rather than relying forever on CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS. Add bounded queries, connection/pool management, timeouts, retries, deployment ownership, load testing, backups and restore tests.
objectives: What you must add before a production custom backend
What a Store or cache does not replace

sections.title: What you must add before a production custom backend
sections.body: Implement explicit schema migrations rather than relying forever on `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`. Add bounded queries, connection/pool management, timeouts, retries, deployment ownership, load testing, backups and restore tests. Define the concurrency contract: a connection lock protects this connection; it does not prevent two application processes from running the same thread. The checkpoint interface evolves. Newer channel types may require ancestor-write reconstruction, and optional operations include pruning/copying. This sample raises an explicit error for delta history instead of silently claiming support. Use an appropriate maintained backend when those features are needed. **Run:** `python labs.py custom` and `python -m pytest -q`. ### Complete custom saver implementation, inline Read the constructor and table definitions first, then `put`, `get_tuple`, `put_writes`, history, deletion, and async adapters. This entire class is defined in the notebook; its examples below use this definition. ```python """Teaching saver with application-owned table names and full checkpoint payloads. For ordinary StateGraph channels. Deliberately excludes DeltaChannel, pruning, thread copying, distributed locking and a native asynchronous database driver. See docs/11_custom_saver.md before adapting this to a production database. """ from __future__ import annotations import asyncio import re import sqlite3 import threading from collections.abc import AsyncIterator, Iterator, Sequence from typing import Any from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableConfig from langgraph.checkpoint.base import ( WRITES_IDX_MAP, BaseCheckpointSaver, ChannelVersions, Checkpoint, CheckpointMetadata, CheckpointTuple, get_checkpoint_metadata, ) from langgraph.checkpoint.serde.base import SerializerProtocol class CustomSqliteSaver(BaseCheckpointSaver[int]): """One locked connection; custom tables; typed payloads; sync + thread adapters.""" def __init__(self, path: str, *, prefix: str = "acme", serde: SerializerProtocol | None = None): super().__init__(serde=serde) if not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]{0,39}", prefix): raise ValueError("prefix must be a short trusted SQL identifier") self.snapshots = f'"{prefix}_snapshots"' self.writes = f'"{prefix}_task_writes"' self.conn = sqlite3.connect(path, check_same_thread=False, timeout=30) self.conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row self.lock = threading.RLock() self.conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL") self.conn.execute("PRAGMA synchronous=FULL") self.conn.executescript(f""" CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS {self.snapshots} ( thread_id TEXT NOT NULL, checkpoint_ns TEXT NOT NULL, checkpoint_id TEXT NOT NULL, parent_checkpoint_id TEXT, checkpoint_type TEXT NOT NULL, checkpoint_payload BLOB NOT NULL, metadata_type TEXT NOT NULL, metadata_payload BLOB NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id) ); CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS {self.writes} ( thread_id TEXT NOT NULL, checkpoint_ns TEXT NOT NULL, checkpoint_id TEXT NOT NULL, task_id TEXT NOT NULL, task_path TEXT NOT NULL, write_index INTEGER NOT NULL, channel TEXT NOT NULL, value_type TEXT NOT NULL, value_payload BLOB NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id, task_id, write_index) ); """) def __enter__(self): return self def __exit__(self, *_): self.close() def close(self): with self.lock: self.conn.close() @staticmethod def _keys(config): c = config["configurable"] thread, ns = c["thread_id"], c.get("checkpoint_ns", "") if not isinstance(thread, str) or not isinstance(ns, str): raise ValueError("thread_id and checkpoint_ns must be strings") return thread, ns @staticmethod def _config(thread, ns, checkpoint_id): return {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread, "checkpoint_ns": ns, "checkpoint_id": checkpoint_id}} def _tuple(self, row): thread, ns, cid = row["thread_id"], row["checkpoint_ns"], row["checkpoint_id"] pending = self.conn.execute( f"SELECT * FROM {self.writes} WHERE thread_id=? AND checkpoint_ns=? " "AND checkpoint_id=? ORDER BY task_path, task_id, write_index", (thread, ns, cid), ).fetchall() parent = row["parent_checkpoint_id"] return CheckpointTuple( config=self._config(thread, ns, cid), checkpoint=self.serde.loads_typed( (row["checkpoint_type"], row["checkpoint_payload"])), metadata=self.serde.loads_typed( (row["metadata_type"], row["metadata_payload"])), parent_config=self._config(thread, ns, parent) if parent else None, pending_writes=[ (w["task_id"], w["channel"], self.serde.loads_typed( (w["value_type"], w["value_payload"]))) for w in pending ], ) def get_tuple(self, config: RunnableConfig) -> CheckpointTuple | None: thread, ns = self._keys(config) cid = config["configurable"].get("checkpoint_id") query = f"SELECT * FROM {self.snapshots} WHERE thread_id=? AND checkpoint_ns=?" args: list[Any] = [thread, ns] if cid is not None: query += " AND checkpoint_id=?" args.append(cid) query += " ORDER BY checkpoint_id DESC LIMIT 1" with self.lock: row = self.conn.execute(query, args).fetchone() return self._tuple(row) if row else None def list(self, config: RunnableConfig | None, *, filter=None, before=None, limit=None) -> Iterator[CheckpointTuple]: clauses, args = [], [] if config is not None: thread, _ = self._keys(config) clauses.append("thread_id=?") args.append(thread) # Omitted namespace lists all namespaces; explicit '' lists the root. for key in ("checkpoint_ns", "checkpoint_id"): if key in config["configurable"]: clauses.append(f"{key}=?") # key is from this constant tuple args.append(config["configurable"][key]) if before is not None: clauses.append("checkpoint_id < ?") args.append(before["configurable"]["checkpoint_id"]) if limit is not None and limit < 0: raise ValueError("limit must be nonnegative") query = f"SELECT * FROM {self.snapshots}" if clauses: query += " WHERE " + " AND ".join(clauses) query += " ORDER BY checkpoint_id DESC" # Teaching implementation: filters metadata in Python, then applies limit. # A large installation should index an allowlisted subset of metadata. with self.lock: items = [] for row in self.conn.execute(query, args).fetchall(): item = self._tuple(row) if filter and any(item.metadata.get(k) != v for k, v in filter.items()): continue if limit is not None and len(items) >= limit: break items.append(item) yield from items def put(self, config: RunnableConfig, checkpoint: Checkpoint, metadata: CheckpointMetadata, new_versions: ChannelVersions) -> RunnableConfig: thread, ns = self._keys(config) cp_type, cp_bytes = self.serde.dumps_typed(checkpoint) meta_type, meta_bytes = self.serde.dumps_typed(get_checkpoint_metadata(config, metadata)) # new_versions is unused because this design stores a complete payload. with self.lock, self.conn: self.conn.execute( f"INSERT INTO {self.snapshots} VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?) " "ON CONFLICT(thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id) DO UPDATE SET " "parent_checkpoint_id=excluded.parent_checkpoint_id, " "checkpoint_type=excluded.checkpoint_type, " "checkpoint_payload=excluded.checkpoint_payload, " "metadata_type=excluded.metadata_type, metadata_payload=excluded.metadata_payload", (thread, ns, checkpoint["id"], config["configurable"].get("checkpoint_id"), cp_type, cp_bytes, meta_type, meta_bytes), ) return self._config(thread, ns, checkpoint["id"]) def put_writes(self, config: RunnableConfig, writes: Sequence[tuple[str, Any]], task_id: str, task_path: str = "") -> None: thread, ns = self._keys(config) cid = config["configurable"]["checkpoint_id"] # Match the pinned SQLite saver's batch policy for reserved control writes. replace = all(channel in WRITES_IDX_MAP for channel, _ in writes) conflict = ( "DO UPDATE SET task_path=excluded.task_path, channel=excluded.channel, " "value_type=excluded.value_type, value_payload=excluded.value_payload" if replace else "DO NOTHING" ) rows = [] for idx, (channel, value) in enumerate(writes): type_, payload = self.serde.dumps_typed(value) rows.append((thread, ns, cid, task_id, task_path, WRITES_IDX_MAP.get(channel, idx), channel, type_, payload)) with self.lock, self.conn: self.conn.executemany( f"INSERT INTO {self.writes} VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?) " "ON CONFLICT(thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id, task_id, write_index) " + conflict, rows, ) def delete_thread(self, thread_id: str) -> None: # Both tables and every namespace are removed in one local transaction. with self.lock, self.conn: self.conn.execute(f"DELETE FROM {self.writes} WHERE thread_id=?", (thread_id,)) self.conn.execute(f"DELETE FROM {self.snapshots} WHERE thread_id=?", (thread_id,)) def get_delta_channel_history(self, **kwargs): raise NotImplementedError("Teaching saver excludes DeltaChannel; use a supported built-in saver") async def aget_delta_channel_history(self, **kwargs): raise NotImplementedError("Teaching saver excludes DeltaChannel; use a supported built-in saver") async def aget_tuple(self, config): return await asyncio.to_thread(self.get_tuple, config) async def alist(self, config, *, filter=None, before=None, limit=None) -> AsyncIterator[CheckpointTuple]: items = await asyncio.to_thread( lambda: list(self.list(config, filter=filter, before=before, limit=limit))) for item in items: yield item async def aput(self, config, checkpoint, metadata, new_versions): return await asyncio.to_thread(self.put, config, checkpoint, metadata, new_versions) async def aput_writes(self, config, writes, task_id, task_path=""): await asyncio.to_thread(self.put_writes, config, writes, task_id, task_path) async def adelete_thread(self, thread_id): await asyncio.to_thread(self.delete_thread, thread_id) ``` ### Run the three examples for this chapter The complete implementation is below. Numbered comments identify the three examples, and assertions check the behavior explained above. ```python def custom_examples(): with TemporaryDirectory() as tmp: path = str(Path(tmp) / "custom.db") # 1. Application-owned table prefix and a durable state value. with CustomSqliteSaver(path, prefix="orders") as saver: counter_graph(saver).invoke({"count": 5}, config("custom")) names = {r[0] for r in saver.conn.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master")} assert "orders_snapshots" in names and "orders_task_writes" in names with CustomSqliteSaver(path, prefix="orders") as saver: assert counter_graph(saver).get_state(config("custom")).values["count"] == 6 print("1. Custom orders_* tables survive reconnecting.") # 2. Failure recovery exercises put_writes, not just put/get. print("2. Custom saver pending-write recovery:", parallel_recovery(saver)) # 3. Audit/filter/delete with the same interface. graph = counter_graph(saver) graph.invoke({"count": 10}, {**config("audit"), "metadata": {"purpose": "demo"}}) records = list(saver.list(config("audit"), filter={"purpose": "demo"}, limit=2)) assert len(records) == 2 saver.delete_thread("audit") assert not list(saver.list(config("audit"))) print("3. Metadata filtering, history limits and thread deletion passed.") ``` ```python custom_examples() ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Many requests for “my own checkpoint table” actually mean a table that analysts
can query: order status, approval result, summary, timestamps and customer ID.
The runtime's checkpoint layout is optimized for execution recovery, not that
reporting format. You can maintain both.

The runnable [export_snapshots.py](checkpointers_masterclass/export_snapshots.py) uses built-in SQLite
checkpoint storage and a second database with `business_snapshot_audit`. The
export contains selected application fields and checkpoint identity. It is a
reporting projection and cannot by itself resume the graph.

sections.title: Example 1 — Export each historical snapshot into your own table
sections.body:
```sql
CREATE TABLE business_snapshot_audit (
    tenant_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    thread_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    checkpoint_ns TEXT NOT NULL,
    checkpoint_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    parent_checkpoint_id TEXT,
    created_at TEXT,
    state_json TEXT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id)
);
```

The script iterates `graph.get_state_history(c)`, projects `count`, and writes JSON
plus snapshot identity. It preserves the parent ID for lineage. The input-stage
checkpoint may not yet have a public count, so its projection uses JSON null.

For your application, replace `count` with an explicit selection such as
`order_id`, `status`, `total`, `approved_by` and `summary`. Avoid automatically
copying every future state field into an analytics database. Explicit projection
makes format changes and sensitive-data handling easier to review.

sections.title: Example 2 — Re-run the export without duplicates
sections.body:
The script exports the same history twice. Its composite primary key and
`INSERT OR IGNORE` keep the row count unchanged. This is useful after a worker
crashes halfway through export: it can repeat the operation.

For PostgreSQL, a business table might look like:

```sql
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS reporting;
CREATE TABLE reporting.agent_snapshot_audit (
    tenant_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    thread_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    checkpoint_ns TEXT NOT NULL,
    checkpoint_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    parent_checkpoint_id TEXT,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    application_schema_version INTEGER NOT NULL,
    public_state JSONB NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id)
);
```

Use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` for immutable exports, or a versioned
projection strategy if transformations change. Reusing a checkpoint ID with
different projection code should be a deliberate migration, not an accidental
silent replacement.

sections.title: Example 3 — Report across conversations while preserving lineage
sections.body: The script exports `audit-one` and `audit-two`, then groups rows by thread ID. Both have separate histories even though the tenant is the same. A useful business query can filter the tenant and join checkpoint identity to your conversation/workflow registry. If you export only after successful completion, failed/paused executions may never reach that export call. For an operational dashboard, export after every invocation outcome or use a background reconciler that scans newly persisted checkpoints. Design the reconciler to be idempotent and tolerate retries. Two databases do not commit atomically just because one Python function writes both. The graph may commit while export fails. Make the checkpoint store the runtime source of truth and allow the reporting view to catch up, or design an explicit transactional outbox if your business requires stronger coordination. Checkpoint ID ordering is useful for traversal; timestamps alone are not unique IDs. Forked histories also require parent links or an explicit selected head. “Latest exported row” and “approved business result” are not necessarily the same. **Run all three:** `python export_snapshots.py`. ### Full snapshot-export implementation and three examples These cells create temporary runtime/business databases and demonstrate export, duplicate-safe re-export, and reporting across two threads. ```python def export_history(graph, c, conn, tenant_id): conn.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS business_snapshot_audit ( tenant_id TEXT NOT NULL, thread_id TEXT NOT NULL, checkpoint_ns TEXT NOT NULL, checkpoint_id TEXT NOT NULL, parent_checkpoint_id TEXT, created_at TEXT, state_json TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id) )""") with conn: for snapshot in graph.get_state_history(c): cfg = snapshot.config["configurable"] parent = snapshot.parent_config # Project only your public state. Messages would need explicit # conversion; never fall back to str() for arbitrary runtime objects. state = {"count": snapshot.values.get("count")} conn.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO business_snapshot_audit VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", (tenant_id, cfg["thread_id"], cfg.get("checkpoint_ns", ""), cfg["checkpoint_id"], parent["configurable"]["checkpoint_id"] if parent else None, snapshot.created_at, json.dumps(state))) def snapshot_export_examples(): with TemporaryDirectory() as tmp: # Three examples: export, repeat idempotently, compare separate threads. with SqliteSaver.from_conn_string(str(Path(tmp) / "runtime.db")) as saver: graph = counter_graph(saver) with closing(sqlite3.connect(str(Path(tmp) / "business.db"))) as conn: graph.invoke({"count": 10}, config("audit-one")) export_history(graph, config("audit-one"), conn, "acme") first = conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM business_snapshot_audit").fetchone()[0] assert first >= 3 print("1. Exported", first, "snapshots to a business-owned table.") export_history(graph, config("audit-one"), conn, "acme") assert conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM business_snapshot_audit").fetchone()[0] == first print("2. Re-export produced no duplicate rows.") graph.invoke({"count": 20}, config("audit-two")) export_history(graph, config("audit-two"), conn, "acme") rows = conn.execute("SELECT thread_id, COUNT(*) FROM business_snapshot_audit GROUP BY thread_id").fetchall() assert len(rows) == 2 print("3. Per-thread audit counts:", rows) ``` ```python snapshot_export_examples() ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
An async Python API, asynchronous checkpoint persistence, and asynchronous user
approval describe three different things. Choose them independently.

| Choice | What it controls |
|---|---|
| `invoke` vs `ainvoke` | Synchronous or asynchronous application call |
| `stream` vs `astream` | How the application consumes execution output |
| `durability='sync'/'async'/'exit'` | When the runtime waits for checkpoint persistence |
| `interrupt()` | Whether execution pauses for an external response |
| Database durability configuration | What survives service/machine failure |

sections.title: Example 1 — Await graph work using an async SQLite saver
sections.body:
```python
async with AsyncSqliteSaver.from_conn_string("data/async.db") as saver:
    graph = counter_graph(saver)
    result = await graph.ainvoke({"count": 10}, config("async"), durability="sync")
    snapshot = await graph.aget_state(config("async"))
```

The lab uses an in-memory SQLite connection and confirms count 11. Here
`ainvoke` lets your application use asyncio, while `durability='sync'` asks the
runtime to await persistence before advancing. There is no contradiction.

Use the asynchronous saver methods with asynchronous graph execution.
`SqliteSaver` is not a substitute for `AsyncSqliteSaver`. Close the saver only
after all graph work that uses it has completed. A graph object does not keep a
closed database connection usable.

In a notebook with a running event loop, use `await async_examples()` instead of
calling `asyncio.run` inside that loop. The command-line lab uses `asyncio.run`
because it owns the process's top-level event loop.

sections.title: Example 2 — Stream updates while checkpointing continues underneath
sections.body:
```python
async for event in graph.astream(
    {"count": 20}, config("stream"), stream_mode="updates"
):
    print(event)
```

The lab sees `{'increment': {'count': 21}}`. That is a node-update event, not a
complete serialized checkpoint. Token/message streaming also does not imply
that a new resumable database checkpoint exists after every token.

If the client disconnects from an HTTP stream, your server's cancellation and
background-job design determines whether graph execution stops. A checkpointer
does not automatically turn a request into a managed background job. To resume,
read the saved thread state and use the appropriate continuation call.

The current docs also describe `stream_events(..., version='v3')` with separate
event projections. This course uses the supported stream-mode API to keep the
small examples straightforward. See the
[streaming reference](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/streaming).

sections.title: Example 3 — Choose when to wait for persistence
sections.body: ```python for mode in ("sync", "async", "exit"): result = await graph.ainvoke(inputs, config(mode), durability=mode) ``` | Mode | Runtime behavior | Example use | |---|---|---| | `sync` | Waits for checkpoint persistence before advancing | Reviewed workflow where recovery precision matters | | `async` | Allows checkpoint I/O to overlap following work | Interactive workflow accepting a small crash window | | `exit` | Defers persistence until execution exits, including controlled errors/interrupts | Work where intermediate crash recovery is unnecessary | A normal return succeeds in all three local examples. That test is not evidence of equal crash resilience. Abrupt process termination can prevent pending writes from reaching storage. A RAM saver loses data on restart even in `sync` mode. Database WAL, replication and storage failure behavior add another durability layer. The supported modes are described in the [checkpoint durability guide](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/checkpointers#durability-modes). **Run:** `python labs.py async`. ### Run the three examples for this chapter The complete implementation is below. Numbered comments identify the three examples, and assertions check the behavior explained above. ```python async def async_examples(): # 1. True async saver lifecycle; close only after awaiting all graph calls. async with AsyncSqliteSaver.from_conn_string(":memory:") as saver: graph = counter_graph(saver) result = await graph.ainvoke({"count": 10}, config("async"), durability="sync") assert result["count"] == 11 assert (await graph.aget_state(config("async"))).values["count"] == 11 print("1. Async invocation and inspection passed.") # 2. UI updates are graph events; checkpoint durability is separate. events = [event async for event in graph.astream( {"count": 20}, config("stream"), stream_mode="updates")] assert any("increment" in event for event in events) print("2. Stream events:", events) # 3. Each durability mode returns correct final state on normal completion. # This demonstrates usage, not a crash-durability benchmark. for mode in ("sync", "async", "exit"): graph = counter_graph(InMemorySaver()) assert (await graph.ainvoke({"count": 1}, config(mode), durability=mode))["count"] == 2 print("3. sync/async/exit completed; RAM is still not crash-persistent.") ``` ```python await async_examples() ```

sections.title: Example 1 — A child graph inherits its parent's checkpointer
sections.body:
The `composition` lab compiles a child without an explicit saver, adds it as a
parent node, and compiles the parent with `InMemorySaver`.

```python
child = child_builder.compile()
parent_builder.add_node("child", child)
graph = parent_builder.compile(checkpointer=saver)
```

The child adds two to count 1, yielding 3. Saver history includes root records
under `''` and child records under a generated `child:...` namespace. Shared state
keys allow the child to return updates through normal graph composition.

Current subgraph persistence choices include inheriting per-invocation behavior,
opting into per-thread child memory with `checkpointer=True`, and disabling child
checkpointing with `checkpointer=False`. The parent still needs the persistence
configuration required for the intended operation. A persistent child called
concurrently can need special care over namespaces and repeated invocation.
Use the [subgraph guide](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/use-subgraphs)
for the exact mode supported by your version.

Inspect with `graph.get_state(c, subgraphs=True)` when child state is available,
especially while interrupted. A child function invoked opaquely inside a tool
is not necessarily exposed like a child added directly as a graph node. Test
the exact composition used by your application.

sections.title: Example 2 — Share a preference across two separate threads
sections.body:
```python
store = InMemoryStore()
namespace = ("tenant-a", "user-7", "preferences")
store.put(namespace, "language", {"value": "Telugu"})
```

Two conversation threads read that same preference and both return Telugu. Their
checkpoint histories remain separate. The Store's key/value namespace models a
durable user fact; it is not a checkpoint namespace.

The lab's node closes over a Store for simplicity and also passes it at compile
time. A larger application can access the configured Store through supported
runtime injection. `InMemoryStore` is still RAM, so choose a persistent Store
backend when preferences must survive process restarts. A checkpointer does not
automatically save arbitrary variables held outside graph state.

Use checkpoint state for the current conversation's working data and a Store for
cross-thread memory you intentionally read/write. See
[Stores](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/stores).

sections.title: Example 3 — Give a LangChain agent the same persistence interface
sections.body:
```python
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain_core.language_models.fake_chat_models import FakeListChatModel

agent = create_agent(
    model=FakeListChatModel(responses=["First reply", "Second reply"]),
    tools=[],
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),
)
```

Calling this agent twice with two new user messages and the same thread yields
four messages. The fake model is deliberately a no-tool model; it demonstrates
the memory wiring without a network call or provider dependency.

For a real agent, replace it with a chat model that supports your desired tools,
install its provider package, and configure credentials outside graph state. The
checkpointer can likewise be replaced with a database saver whose context stays
open for the agent's lifetime. `create_agent` produces graph-based behavior;
older generic chains or independent LCEL runnables do not automatically acquire
this state machinery.

sections.title: What a Store or cache does not replace
sections.body: A vector store retrieves documents; it is not automatically a checkpoint saver. A model cache reuses model results; it does not represent where the workflow paused. A chat-history table stores messages; it does not necessarily preserve tasks, routing or replay history. Each can coexist with a checkpointer. **Run:** `python labs.py composition`. ### Run the three examples for this chapter The complete implementation is below. Numbered comments identify the three examples, and assertions check the behavior explained above. ```python def composition(): # 1. A child graph inherits the parent's saver; inspect saved namespaces. child = StateGraph(CounterState).add_node("child_step", lambda s: {"count": s["count"] + 2}) child = child.add_edge(START, "child_step").add_edge("child_step", END).compile() parent = StateGraph(CounterState).add_node("child", child).add_edge(START, "child").add_edge("child", END) saver = InMemorySaver() graph = parent.compile(checkpointer=saver) assert graph.invoke({"count": 1}, config("parent"))["count"] == 3 namespaces = {t.config["configurable"]["checkpoint_ns"] for t in saver.list(config("parent"))} assert "" in namespaces and any(ns.startswith("child:") for ns in namespaces) print("1. Root and child namespaces:", sorted(namespaces)) # 2. A Store namespace shares a preference across two conversation threads. store = InMemoryStore() store.put(("tenant-a", "user-7", "preferences"), "language", {"value": "Telugu"}) class Preference(TypedDict): language: str def read_preference(_): return {"language": store.get(("tenant-a", "user-7", "preferences"), "language").value["value"]} g = StateGraph(Preference).add_node("read", read_preference).add_edge(START, "read").add_edge("read", END) g = g.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver(), store=store) for thread in ("conversation-1", "conversation-2"): assert g.invoke({}, config(thread))["language"] == "Telugu" print("2. Two threads read one user preference from a Store.") # 3. LangChain create_agent accepts the same checkpointer interface. # A deterministic no-tool chat model keeps this example free of network calls. from langchain.agents import create_agent from langchain_core.language_models.fake_chat_models import FakeListChatModel agent = create_agent(model=FakeListChatModel(responses=["First reply", "Second reply"]), tools=[], checkpointer=InMemorySaver()) c = config("langchain-agent") agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]}, c) out = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Continue"}]}, c) assert len(out["messages"]) == 4 print("3. LangChain agent retained both turns using a LangGraph saver.") ``` ```python composition() ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
The saver must turn Python runtime values into a durable representation and
reconstruct compatible values later. The serializer contract uses
`dumps_typed(value) -> (type_name, bytes)` and
`loads_typed((type_name, bytes)) -> value`.

Keep serializer compatibility separate from database DDL compatibility and
application state-schema compatibility. Changing any one can affect resuming
old threads.

sections.title: Example 1 — Preserve a message's type and identity
sections.body:
```python
serde = JsonPlusSerializer()
encoded = serde.dumps_typed(HumanMessage(content="Hello", id="msg-1"))
restored = serde.loads_typed(encoded)
assert isinstance(restored, HumanMessage)
assert restored.id == "msg-1"
```

If you simply called `str(message)` before storing it, you would preserve a text
representation rather than a usable message object. Message IDs participate in
the reducer's replacement behavior, so losing them can change application
semantics after reload.

Use the pinned library's typed serializer for runtime payloads. Keep checkpoint
storage restricted to trusted writers. Review allowlisting/strict deserialization
controls when enabling application-specific classes; serialization is a data
boundary, not a reason to accept arbitrary user-supplied serialized objects.

sections.title: Example 2 — Preserve datetimes and bytes
sections.body:
The lab round-trips a UTC datetime and `b'abc'` without converting them into vague
strings. A plain `json.dumps` cannot encode these values without custom handling.
Conversely, your business audit projection can deliberately convert datetimes to
ISO text and message objects to selected JSON fields because it has a different
purpose from runtime reconstruction.

Do not enable pickle fallback merely to silence a serialization error. Prefer
simple state values and explicit representations. Pickle-based deserialization
requires a trusted payload source and introduces compatibility/security concerns.
Encrypted storage does not make a malicious authenticated writer trustworthy.

An optional encrypted-saver configuration uses the provided serializer wrapper:

```python
# Optional dependency: pycryptodome. Use a fresh secure key from secret storage.
import base64
import os
from langgraph.checkpoint.serde.encrypted import EncryptedSerializer

key = base64.b64decode(os.environ["CHECKPOINT_AES_KEY_B64"])
serde = EncryptedSerializer.from_pycryptodome_aes(key=key)
with CustomSqliteSaver("encrypted.db", serde=serde) as saver:
    graph = counter_graph(saver)
```

This is a configuration recipe, not one of the executed core lab assertions.
Keep keys outside state and source code; retain a key-version/rotation plan.
The wrapper encrypts payloads passed through it. Thread IDs, table keys, metadata
columns or other fields stored separately by a backend may remain readable.
Inspect the chosen backend before claiming complete field-level confidentiality.

sections.title: Example 3 — Save a document reference rather than an open resource
sections.body: ```python state_fragment = { "document_uri": "documents/invoice-7.pdf", "sha256": "demo-hash", "page": 3, } ``` The lab round-trips this plain dictionary. The node that needs the PDF opens it again using the saved reference. A real hash verifies that the same content is being processed on recovery; the sample string is only a placeholder. Database connections, socket objects, generators, open files and model clients belong in runtime dependencies, not saved state. Large document bodies and image bytes can make every checkpoint expensive; save object references and content versions where practical. Ensure the referenced object survives as long as the workflow can be resumed. **Run:** `python labs.py serialization`. For serializer classes and encryption interfaces, see the [checkpoint reference](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/reference/checkpoints/). ### Run the three examples for this chapter The complete implementation is below. Numbered comments identify the three examples, and assertions check the behavior explained above. ```python def serialization(): from datetime import datetime, timezone from langgraph.checkpoint.serde.jsonplus import JsonPlusSerializer serde = JsonPlusSerializer() # 1. Messages preserve type and identity across typed serialization. type_, payload = serde.dumps_typed(HumanMessage(content="Hello", id="msg-1")) restored = serde.loads_typed((type_, payload)) assert isinstance(restored, HumanMessage) and restored.id == "msg-1" print("1. Message type and ID survived serialization.") # 2. Datetime/bytes values are richer than a naive JSON-only state dump. value = {"at": datetime(2026, 10, 28, tzinfo=timezone.utc), "blob": b"abc"} assert serde.loads_typed(serde.dumps_typed(value)) == value print("2. Datetime and bytes round-tripped.") # 3. Store a document reference, not a live file/socket/database connection. value = {"document_uri": "documents/invoice-7.pdf", "sha256": "demo-hash", "page": 3} assert serde.loads_typed(serde.dumps_typed(value)) == value print("3. A plain reference payload round-tripped.") ``` ```python serialization() ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
These are application designs built from the runnable components in this course.
They are not a deployed API service. The details below explain the extra work
between a working notebook and a reliable multi-user application.

sections.title: Example 1 — A web API with stable threads and one shared pool
sections.body:
**Scenario:** a chat API has three worker processes and must resume approval after
a deployment.

At startup, each process opens its database pool and constructs a compatible
saver and graph. At request time, authenticate the user, look up the requested
conversation in your own registry, confirm tenant ownership, and derive the
internal thread ID. Pass only allowlisted configuration into the graph.

```text
POST /conversations/{id}/messages
  -> authorize conversation
  -> enqueue/serialize work for its thread
  -> graph.ainvoke(new_message_dict, authorized_config)

GET /conversations/{id}/state
  -> authorize conversation
  -> graph.aget_state(authorized_config)
  -> return selected fields and pending review details

POST /conversations/{id}/review
  -> authorize reviewer and validate response
  -> verify review/checkpoint is still pending
  -> graph.ainvoke(Command(resume=response), authorized_config)
```

Store the mapping from public conversation IDs to internal thread IDs in your
application database. Validate that a late review refers to the still-current
pending operation; otherwise a response to yesterday's review could be applied
to today's different pause.

The graph call belongs inside the saver/pool lifetime. Shutdown waits for
in-flight work or cancels it under a known recovery policy, then closes resources.
`database_recipes.py:postgres_pool` provides the pool wiring; `restart_demo.py`
demonstrates persistent approval independently of an HTTP framework.

When using a managed Agent Server, persistence may be owned by that server. Use
its supported thread/run and custom-checkpointer configuration instead of
assuming local `compile(checkpointer=...)` controls deployment storage. See
[persistence and Agent Server](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence).
